The Meiji Emancipation Edict of 1871 abolished the senmin status categories, including eta and hinin. Alastair McLaughlan states it plainly: “Formal discrimination against all outcastes was abolished by the new Meiji government’s 1871 Eta Emancipation Edict (Eta Kaiho Rei)” (McLaughlan 2006, 1).

In the same period the Household Registration Law produced the registers on which the modern Japanese state was built. David Chapman: “The creation of the jinshin koseki through the Household Registration Law (koseki hō) (introduced in 1871 and implemented in 1872) played a critical role in the formation of a modern state” (Chapman 2011). Karl Jakob Krogness records that the 1872 registers “required that each administrative household be identified by family class (zokushō),” with entries for nobility, samurai, lower samurai, peasant, artisan and merchant, categories that “perpetuated the status pattern of Edo era society” and were abolished only in 1947 (Krogness 2014).

The decisive detail is a separate one, and the two claims should not be run together. Krogness’s zokushō categories do not include a former-outcaste entry. What marked the emancipated was a different notation. Chapman: “the new registries labelled the former outcaste households with the term ‘new commoner’ or ‘original eta’ (shinheimin/motoeta) maintaining an identifiable differentiated status” (Chapman 2011). Amos and his co-authors describe the same designation as one that “legally marked particular communities in relation to their former outcaste origins in ways that continued to affect the households long into the postwar period” (Amos et al. 2021), and note that the 1872 registers “are particularly problematic documents for Burakumin as they can be used to demonstrate beyond much doubt the connections between particular individuals and outcaste ancestry.” The register therefore outlived the status by more than a century as a working instrument. Krogness gives the timetable in a single passage: “Access to koseki copies have only very gradually been limited, beginning in the late 1960s. Not until 2008 did it become required for everyone, including the person in question, to show ID when requesting a koseki copy” (Krogness 2014). Chapman dates a particular legislative reform on public access to 1976; the two are steps in the same process rather than competing dates. The most evident instance is the Buraku Chimei Sōkan, a directory of buraku locations compiled for employment screening. An anonymous letter delivered to the Buraku Liberation League in Osaka on 18 November 1975 exposed it, and the scandal broke at a press conference on 9 December. According to the League’s own research institute, 223 corporations purchased copies, some of them several (Buraku Liberation and Human Rights Research Institute, Buraku Liberation News 137). The directory is distinct from the 1936 Zenkoku Buraku Chōsa survey data, which became the subject of separate litigation in 2016.

An emancipation edict that abolishes a status and at the same time produces the record by which its former holders can be identified in perpetuity is structurally the same event as Madagascar in 1896, with the addition of paperwork, twenty-five years earlier, and with no European involvement.

The parallel points to something more general about how closure works when the mark is not visible. Neither buraku descent nor Malagasy mainty descent can be seen. Erving Goffman’s distinction between a discredited stigma, already evident to those present, and a discreditable one, concealable but ruinous if discovered, identifies the problem exactly: where the stigma is discreditable, the stigmatised person’s difficulty is managing information, and the stigmatiser’s difficulty is acquiring it (Goffman 1963). Bureaucracy is the institutional solution to the second. Where the eye cannot do the work of classification an archive does it, and racial classification becomes a documentary practice rather than an optical one. Keith Breckenridge’s phrase for the South African population register, “bureaucratically formed descent,” names the same thing (Breckenridge 2014). This is the point at which the thesis’s portability claim can be stated with more precision. A discreditable closure is necessarily local, because the archive that sustains it is local. A koseki is legible in Japan and nowhere else. What distinguishes anti-Blackness is that its mark is discredited rather than discreditable, carried on the body rather than in a register, and therefore portable without any administrative infrastructure at all. That is not a claim about the moral seriousness of the two closures. It is a claim about their geography.
Three Doors

Three explanations are commonly offered for the persistence of racial inequality which would, if correct, dispense with any account like this one. Each proposes an alternative variable: class, gender, religion. On the present argument they are not three competing explanations but three instances of a single finding, because each names a route out that does not function.

Class. Devah Pager’s audit study of Milwaukee employers found callback rates of 34 per cent for white applicants without a criminal record and 17 per cent for white applicants with a felony conviction; among black applicants without records, only 14 per cent received callbacks (Pager 2003, 955, 957–58). Her own summary is exact: “In fact, even whites with criminal records received more favorable treatment (17%) than blacks without criminal records (14%)” (Pager 2003, 958). Marianne Bertrand and Sendhil Mullainathan’s correspondence study found that “White names receive 50 percent more callbacks for interviews,” and, in the more consequential finding, that “Callbacks are also more responsive to resume quality for White names than for African-American ones” (Bertrand and Mullainathan 2004, 991). On wealth, William Darity and colleagues report that “on average, a black household with a college-educated head has less wealth than a white family whose head did not even obtain a high school diploma” (Darity et al. 2018, 5–6).

These findings are usually read as evidence that racial disadvantage is not reducible to class. They can be read with more precision than that. What they describe is a door. The meritocratic route out, by credential and by conduct, is available, is used, and does not open. The second of Bertrand and Mullainathan’s findings is the one of greatest utility to this thesis, and it tends to be under-quoted: it is not simply that a Black applicant starts further back, but that improving the application returns less. That is the difference between a handicap and a closure, and it is the empirical form of the distinction drawn in the Introduction between movement within a position and departure from it.

Gender. Hortense Spillers’s account of the Middle Passage argues that under the conditions of captivity gender does not survive as a category: “Under these conditions, we lose at least gender difference in the outcome, and the female body and the male body become a territory of cultural and political maneuver, not at all gender-related, gender-specific” (Spillers 1987, 67). Page references to Spillers are to the original Diacritics printing. On Isabell Dahms’s reading, which I follow, the claim is not that black women were excluded from an existing category of womanhood but rather that gender assignment was suspended: “most notable is the suspension of gender and sex-role assignation, which, with the exception of the reproductive labour of birthing, do not emerge for enslaved African-Americans in this historic instance” (Dahms 2020).

The consequence for the present argument is that gender was not a door that closed. It was never open. And Spillers’s account of kinship is the theoretical counterpart of the Virginia act of 1662: “I would call this enforced state of breach another instance of vestibular cultural formation where ‘kinship’ loses meaning, since it can be invaded at any given and arbitrary moment by the property relations” (Spillers 1987, 74). Kinship that property can invade at will is not kinship, and a child who inherits condition but not name, lineage or entitlement has no line to be restored to. Compare the Betsileo tomb, which is exactly a line to be restored to, and the reason the Malagasy exit worked while the American one did not.

The comparison with Islamic law made in Chapter I sharpens here. Two legal systems faced the same question about the child of an enslaved mother and chose opposite parents. The Virginia act of December 1662 enacted “that all children borne in this country shalbe held bond or free only according to the condition of the mother,” and in the same sentence doubled the fine for fornication between a Christian and a “negro man or woman” (Hening 1823, II, 170). It thereby made bondage heritable and paternity legally void. The umm al-walad provisions made the master’s paternity determinative and freed both mother and child. The direction in which descent is reckoned is not a technical detail of family law. It is the instrument by which the exit is held open or shut, and it is chosen. Religion. The failure of the religious route is the subject of Chapter III, and its modern form is worth registering because it shows the operation running live. Paragraph 3 of India’s Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order of 1950 provides: “Notwithstanding anything contained in paragraph 2, no person who professes a religion different from the Hindu, the Sikh or the Buddhist religion shall be deemed to be a member of a Scheduled Caste.” Sikhs were added by Act 63 of 1956 and Buddhists by Act 15 of 1990.

In March 2026 the Supreme Court of India applied it. In Chinthada Anand v. State of Andhra Pradesh (2026 INSC 283, decided 24 March 2026) the Court held that “for a person to be recognised as a member of a Scheduled Caste, he must be professing the Hindu religion or such other religions as are expressly recognised under the Constitution (Scheduled Castes) Order, 1950. Once the appellant converted to Christianity, the caste status, which he earlier enjoyed as a member of the Madiga community, stood eclipsed in the eyes of law” (para. 56). The consequence was that he could not invoke the protections of the atrocities legislation. The question before the Court was the narrower one of standing under the Scheduled Castes and Scheduled Tribes (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, and the ruling should be read as a decision on that question rather than as a general pronouncement on Scheduled Caste status.

The structure is the reverse of Virginia’s, since the status in question is a protection rather than a bondage, and the difference should be acknowledged rather than smoothed over. But the logic is the one the Virginia Assembly used in 1667, and it is being applied by a court this year: religion is not permitted to alter what descent has fixed. In 1667 a man could convert and remain a slave. In 2026 a man can convert and cease to be protected. In both cases the conversion is real, permitted, and without effect upon the thing that matters.
What Closure Is, and What Maintains It

It would be tempting to treat the closure of the generational exit as the definition of racialisation. That cannot be sustained. It implies that a society which formally opens the exit thereby stops being racialised, and no reasonable observer of the contemporary United States would accept the implication.
The correction is the one stated in the Introduction: closure is not an event but a practice, which has to be performed continuously, and whose instrument changes. It is worth separating two forms.

Statutory closure shuts the exit by law and names its own agent. Virginia in 1667. Maryland in 1671. The Scheduled Castes Order in 1950. Its characteristic feature is that it is written down, which makes it both effective and vulnerable: a statute can be repealed, and the repeal can be demanded.

Discretionary closure leaves the exit formally open and re-closes it case by case, through the employer who does not call back, the lender, the marriage investigation, the admissions committee, the landlord. No statute is required. More importantly, none is available to contest. The decision is made by a private party who is not obliged to explain it and who, in the individual case, can almost always point to some other reason.

Emancipation does not end closure. It changes the instrument, and it changes it in a particular direction: it removes the form that was easiest to challenge and leaves intact the form that is hardest. That is why abolition is so reliably followed by a period in which everything has changed legally and very little has changed positionally.

Saidiya Hartman arrives at the same point from the other direction. In Scenes of Subjection emancipation “appears less the grand event of liberation than a point of transition between modes of servitude and racial subjection” (Hartman 1997). In her 2022 preface, adapted in The New York Review of Books, she is more explicit: “The restricted vision of freedom offered by the liberal imagination, a vision even more attenuated and hollowed out by counterrevolution, economic predation, antiblack violence, and white supremacy, would not transform the plantation, or abolish racial slavery and its badges or indices, or eradicate caste, or negate the legacy and stigma of having been chattel” (Hartman 2022).

Derrick Bell supplies a mechanism for the cases where the formal exit does open. In his account of Brown v. Board of Education, the “principle of ‘interest convergence’ provides: The interest of blacks in achieving racial equality will be accommodated only when it converges with the interests of whites” (Bell 1980, 523). That is discretionary closure described from the side of the law rather than the side of the labour market. The door is opened when opening it costs nothing, which is also part of the explanation for why opening it changes so little.

This meets what is otherwise the most serious objection to the thesis. Barbara Fields argues that ideology cannot be inherited or transmitted. It is, she writes, “not a material entity, a thing of any sort, that you can hand down like an old garment, pass on like a germ, spread like a rumour, or impose like a code of dress or etiquette” (Fields 1990, 110), and consequently “nothing handed down from the past could keep race alive if we did not constantly reinvent and re-ritualize it to fit our own terrain” (Fields 1990, 117). She is right, and an account in which a closure simply persists by inertia is exactly what she rules out. But the reinvention she demands is observable, and the thesis can point to it. It is Pager’s employers, making decisions in 2001 that nobody made for them in 1667. It is the differential return to a better résumé. It is the koseki request. Closure is not inherited. It is performed, daily, in documented transactions, by people who could in principle be identified. Fields does not address audit studies, and whether she would accept this as meeting her objection is my inference rather than her claim; but it is the kind of reinvention her argument requires, and it is on the record.

The correction also relocates the test of the thesis, and this is the point on which the whole argument should be judged. The question is not whether the exit is open. It is whether the category dissolves. Roman freedman status dissolved: the children were ingenui, full citizens, and descent from a freedman ceased within a few generations to carry legal or social consequence, whatever was shouted at Gabinius. American racial categories do not dissolve. That difference does not depend on whether any particular person escaped, which is why individual mobility, real and in some periods substantial, is entirely compatible with a categorical position that has not moved.
The (Un)Logic Objection

Annie Olaloku-Teriba’s essay is the most direct challenge to what this thesis is attempting, and it is also, in places, its closest ally. Both halves need saying. Her target is Afro-pessimism, and specifically the claim that the slave is paradigmatically black. She finds two axioms buried in it: that the position of the slave is necessarily black, understood morphologically, and that “slaveness links the Negro and the African.” Together they amount to a biological definition of blackness smuggled into a theory that presents itself as structural (Olaloku-Teriba 2018). Against this she argues that blackness was made, and made by policy: “And so, the slave was not created so that the American might exist; instead, the black was created so that slavery might survive republican fervour.”

That sentence is very close to the argument of Chapter III. The Virginia act of 1667 is exactly such a policy-practice, passed to keep a religious criterion from undoing servile status. On this point the thesis and Olaloku-Teriba agree, and her account of measures aimed at the free black population is a useful American instance of closure directed at people who had, in fact, got out. It is the American version of Gardini’s footnote about the mainty.

The disagreement concerns mechanism, and what survives abolition. Olaloku-Teriba, following Fanon, makes exploitation the relation that matters. On her reading, the post-abolition forms that Afro-pessimism calls slavery’s afterlife are better understood as varieties of exploitation, and treating African enslavement as exceptional obscures the fact that the blackness of the category of slave was both contingent and unstable.

The thesis accepts the contingency and rejects the substitution. If exploitation were the mechanism, then improvement in the terms of exploitation, higher wages, better credentials, a clean record, should move people, and should move them proportionally. The evidence in the preceding section is that it does not. Bertrand and Mullainathan’s finding that a better résumé buys a Black applicant less is not a finding about the rate of exploitation; it is a finding about a door. Closure is what exploitation relies upon to decide who can be exploited on which terms, and it is closure rather than exploitation that reproduces the category across the abolition of the relation.

Her strongest counter-case is colonial southern Africa. There, she argues, “the contradiction between legitimacy and accumulation meant that colonial authorities frequently intervened to strengthen the hold of kinship bonds, in order to secure young men’s labour in a system of indirect rule,” so that “the African’s primary relationship to the state was neither as a worker, nor as a black, but as Xhosa, Zulu, et cetera.” If Afro-pessimism defines blackness by the destruction of kinship, this is a serious problem for it. It is less of a problem for the argument made here, which does not define anti-Blackness by natal alienation but by the closure of exits and the portability of the mark. Southern Africa shows closure running through a different instrument, ethnicisation rather than kin destruction, which is the pattern Mahmood Mamdani describes for the colonial state generally (Mamdani 1996). The mark was still portable: the same person classified as a subject of customary law at home was classified as a native in the city.
The Coloured Case, and Who Maintains a Closure
There is also a case within southern Africa where Olaloku-Teriba’s claim does not hold, and it is worth putting because she does not analyse it.

Under apartheid the “Coloured” category was defined residually. The Population Registration Act No. 30 of 1950, section 1, defines a “native” as “a person who in fact is or is generally accepted as a member of any aboriginal race or tribe of Africa,” a “white person” as “a person who in appearance obviously is, or who is generally accepted as a white person,” and a “coloured person” as “a person who is not a white person or a native.” Classification proceeded by appearance and acceptance, with descent added by amendment in 1967, and it was applied to individuals rather than to lineages.

The effect on kinship was the opposite of what Olaloku-Teriba describes for African migrant labour. Deborah Posel records that “many families were ruptured when children of the same parents received different racial classifications, or all children were classified differently from their parents” (Posel 2001). Geoffrey Bowker and Susan Leigh Star, drawing on earlier reports, cite a family in which “one twin was classified as coloured and the other as African,” and the observation that “there are today many families split down the middle” (Horrell 1958, 70, and Doman 1975, 151, quoted in Bowker and Star 1999, 217, 213). The Prohibition of Mixed Marriages Act of 1949 and the Immorality Amendment Act of 1950 prevented new kin ties from forming across the line.

Two things follow. First, the colonial and apartheid state in southern Africa did not have one policy on kinship; it strengthened kinship where kinship could be made to deliver labour through chiefs, and it severed kinship where classification required individuals to be sorted. Olaloku-Teriba’s generalisation holds for the case she takes and not for the adjacent one.

Second, and of more utility to the thesis, the Coloured case is a closure built upon an intermediate position. Mohamed Adhikari describes Coloured people as having “experienced the South African racial hierarchy as a three-tiered system in which they held an intermediate position,” and identifies the basic dynamic behind the assertion of Coloured identity as the defence of that position against relegation to the status of Africans (Adhikari 2006, 477).

That is the beginning of an answer to a question this thesis has otherwise avoided: the extent to which people who are not white maintain anti-Black closure. The answer the Coloured case suggests is that an intermediate position is defended downwards, because its only content is not being the category below it. Zimitri Erasmus’s formulation, which Adhikari quotes, is the sharpest available: not only not white, but less than white; not only not black, but better than black. A closure with an intermediate tier recruits that tier to police the boundary beneath it, and does so without needing to command anything, because the tier’s own interest is sufficient.

The thesis has more material on this question than it has so far gathered in one place, and it is worth naming here rather than leaving it scattered. Hall’s bīḍān and sūdān is a hierarchy among non-white people in which genealogy decides who may be enslaved. Ahmad Bābā did not regard himself as standing on the enslaveable side of the line he was defending, and a student wrote to settle the question. Mawlay Ismāʿīl enslaved black Moroccans in a North African state with no European involvement. The Malagasy fotsy and mainty division operates inside a population that is majority African in ancestry. Set beside the Coloured tier, these are five instances, across four chapters, of closure maintained by people who are not white. That distribution is itself an argument for portability, because a mark that only white people can read is not portable, and the evidence is that it was read everywhere.

Finally, Olaloku-Teriba’s complaint that anti-Blackness has never been defined is one the thesis has tried to answer by offering a definition. Whether closure plus portability is the right one is open to argument. That it is a definition, historically grounded and capable of being wrong, is the point of making it.
What Has Been Argued

The argument has been that racialisation is the closure of an exit rather than the invention of a difference; that the essentialist claim follows the foreclosure rather than causing it; that closure is a practice requiring continuous performance rather than an event with a long half-life; and that what separates anti-Blackness from the many structurally similar closures is that it alone became portable.

The chapters were arranged so that each of those claims would be capable of failing. Chapter I assembled four hierarchies with working exits, so that closure could not be said to be everywhere. Chapter II took the one case where the essentialising narrative can be dated rather than inferred, and found it arriving after the enslaving rather than before it. Chapter III set two legal answers to a single question against each other and found that the society which removed the religious criterion had to install a new one, on a ground that conversion could not cross. Chapter IV followed two emancipations that abolished a status without dissolving the group, and then showed the same operation running in a labour market that has no statute behind it at all.
What Would Show the Argument to Be Wrong
A comparative thesis of this design can only illustrate its theory unless it says what would embarrass it. Four things would.

The first would be evidence that in Rome, or in another society with routine manumission, descent from a freedman did continue to determine legal standing, marriage and office across many generations, and that the category reproduced itself rather than dissolving. That would remove the contrast the whole argument is built on, and would suggest that what distinguishes the Atlantic case is a matter of degree rather than of kind. McKeown’s Gabinius is a small piece of evidence in that direction and has been quoted rather than suppressed.

The second would be evidence that the Curse of Ham in its dual form, blackness and bondage produced by the same act, circulated widely before black Africans were being enslaved in large numbers in the societies where it circulated. Goldenberg’s dating is the load-bearing element of Chapter II, and a redating would break the sequence the thesis depends on.

The third would be a demonstration that returns to credentials, conduct and capital are in fact equal across racial categories once some further variable is controlled for, so that what looks like a door is a difference in what people bring to it. This is the live empirical dispute and the thesis does not pretend to have settled it; it has relied on audit studies precisely because they hold the application constant, and the argument would be in real trouble if that design were shown to be measuring something else.

The fourth would be a well documented case of a closure that was as local as burakumin or andevo status and yet travelled, remaining legible in a society that had no part in making it. That would defeat the portability claim, which is the least established of the four and the one this thesis offers as a proposal rather than a finding.

That last point deserves an honest paragraph rather than a brave one, and I think the thesis is stronger for giving it. What supports portability is the contrast between cases. Converso, burakumin and andevo status were legible only where they were made, while the categories produced by the trans-Saharan, Indian Ocean and Atlantic trades travelled with the people who bore them and stayed legible on arrival. Ahmad Bābā’s captives were seized in West Africa and marked in Morocco, which is exactly why al-Jīrārī’s question was necessary in the first place: the mark arrived before the man’s history did. What would be required to establish the claim properly is a systematic comparison of the conditions under which a mark does and does not survive relocation, and that has not been attempted here. Jonathon Glassman’s account of Zanzibar, which traces the island’s racial divisions to the Omani plantation economy rather than to British rule, would test it more severely than anything in this thesis (Glassman 2011).
On Afro-Pessimism
The position that follows on Afro-pessimism is a qualified one, and the qualification runs in both directions.

Frank Wilderson’s claim that the Black position is not adequately described by the categories of exploitation seems to me correct, and Chapter IV’s account of what class fails to explain is consistent with it. “The worker demands that productivity be fair and democratic (Gramsci’s new hegemony, Lenin’s dictatorship of the proletariat), the slave, on the other hand, demands that production stop; stop without recourse to its ultimate democratisation” (Wilderson 2003, 230). That is also the point on which the thesis parts company with Olaloku-Teriba, who would make exploitation the whole of the relation. His further claim that the position is sui generis, and that social death is an ontology rather than a history, does not follow from the evidence considered here, and Chapter I is the reason. Rome had social death and no surviving category. If social death were the ontological ground of Blackness, Rome should not look the way it looks. The alternative offered here is that the distinctiveness of the Black position lies in scale and portability, both of which have datable historical causes, and that this accounts for the same phenomena without requiring an ontology.

There is a methodological point in this that is worth making explicit, because it applies to the thesis as much as to the theory it is engaging. A transhistorical ontological claim cannot be embarrassed by historical cases, and a framework stated at that level converts every case into an illustration. That is the same trap, arriving from the theory side, that Skocpol and Somers identify on the method side: because the cases are selected in the first place in terms of the given theory, “the juxtaposed historical trajectories are not used to establish controls, only to show the theory at work again and again” (Skocpol and Somers 1980, 191). The reason this thesis states its claim as a historical mechanism with named instruments and datable performances is that a mechanism can be shown not to be operating. An ontology cannot. That a condition presents from the inside as timeless is not evidence that it is timeless, and the phenomenological force of the Afro-pessimist description, which is considerable, is not an argument for its ontological form.
What Remains Open
Several things remain open, and it is better to list them than to leave a reader to find them.

The Malagasy evidence for a pre-colonial ritual exit concerns freed individuals in one southern Betsileo community. Whether slave descendants could be cleansed, and whether the same held in Imerina, is not established, and the disagreement in the literature about whether the mainty were free royal servants or royal slaves has been recorded rather than resolved. The claim that Ahmad Bābā held the religious exit open has to sit beside the fact that he also mapped the peoples still open to enslavement, and his exact wording on the Curse of Ham has been given here through Hall rather than from the translation itself. The ḥarāṭīn, who are the sharpest available instance of a category surviving an open legal exit, have been given a paragraph where they deserve a chapter. The Indian Ocean case has been named and not undertaken. So has the rest of the comparative programme the argument implies: the Sahel after the French abolitions, South Asian caste after the 1950 Order, the Korean nobi.
The Narrow Claim
What can be said with more confidence is narrower, and the thesis ends upon it rather than upon the widest version of its argument.

In 1615 and in 1667, two societies with no knowledge of each other faced the same question about whether faith could carry a person out of bondage. One said that it must, and set out at length why. The other said that it did not, and added that masters should now feel free to evangelise. The second answer left the society that gave it needing something new to mark who could be held, and what it found was descent. Three and a half centuries later the marking no longer requires a statute, no longer names an agent, and no longer has to explain itself. It is performed in a great many small decisions by people who would, almost all of them, deny that they were performing it. That is not the afterlife of a closure. It is the closure, still being carried out.
